catalog_quote: [Abstract] Little research has examined the temporal alignment of co-speech gestures in African tonal languages, where metrical prominence is often hard to identify due to a lack of canonical stress correlates, and where a key function of pitch is in distinguishing between words, rather than marking intonational prominence. ... the final syllable in the word is the default position for gesture alignment in Igbo ... [sec. 1] As is the case for most Niger-Congo languages (particularly those situated in the northwestern region of Sub-Saharan Africa), neither of these languages displays typical acoustic correlates of lexical stress, such as increased vowel duration or intensity. Nonetheless, for both languages, there is some evidence to suggest that word-level metrical prominence asymmetries are present (Clark 1990; Franich 2018, 2021). ... tone is primarily used to encode lexical contrasts in both Medʉmba and Igbo. [sec. 1.2] Specifically, she proposes that the language assigns alternating prominences from the right edge of the word, and that initial metrically-prominent syllables actually resist the linking of the associative high tone (and the subsequent downstep that it would trigger). [sec. 4] In Igbo, on the other hand, word-final position is the strongest attractor of gestures. This finding is in line with work by Clark (1990) arguing for the right-to-left assignment of metrical prominences at the word level in Igbo.

sweep_summary: Igbo (nucl1417) is not in the catalog. Of the five title-hit items, only Anyanwu 2003 'Tone and accent in the Igbo verb' (FAB 15, Köppe; publisher-sold PDF, no DOI, no open copy anywhere I could reach: HathiTrust ISBN lookup empty, archive.org empty, Frankfurt server 403) is squarely about accent placement in Igbo words — high priority, unread. Zsiga 1992 (CUP paywall; abstract read via Crossref) is about prosodic domains via ATR harmony and vowel assimilation, not stress; her open 1997 Language paper on the same rules was downloaded and is silent on stress. Uzochukwu 1981 is verse metre (T&F paywall, no abstract exposed; low). Manfredi 1992 IRCS (held by the project, read) is downstep/downstep-reset in Àgbọ̀ Igbo under a tone-metrical government model — silent on word stress. Ezeriọha 2014 (UNN MA thesis, 101 pp.) could not be located (repository unreachable). Best first-hand statement actually read: Franich, Keupdjio & Nwosu 2025 (Glossa, held by the project) — Igbo shows no acoustic correlates of lexical stress; word-level metrical prominence, per Clark 1990 and the authors' gesture data, is word-final (right-to-left alternating); Franich & Nwosu 2026 (LabPhon) restates Clark's analysis. Clark 1990 (De Gruyter) remains the unread primary source, high priority. DDG, Bing, Brave, Mojeek, Google Scholar, HathiTrust and T&F pages bot-blocked), so discovery relied on Crossref, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Glottolog, Köppe and author sites.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Igbo is a two-tone (H, L + downstep) language with no canonical acoustic stress correlates; the only word-prominence claim is metrical: Clark (1990) assigns alternating prominence right-to-left so the word-final syllable is prominent (and the initial syllable of trisyllables), and Franich et al.'s co-speech-gesture timing data independently pick out the word-final syllable as the default prominent position. No source opened states a conventional word-stress rule; the standard descriptive grammars (Emenanjo 2015, Green & Igwe 1963) could not be opened.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Clark's analysis (as reported) implies alternating prominence leftward from the final syllable, i.e. initial syllable of trisyllabic words also metrically strong; Franich et al. additionally suggest a left-edge prominence at the start of a multiply-linked H tone span ('tonal foot').
new_statements.exceptions: Words with HH melody (single multiply-linked H) attract gestures to the initial syllable more often; prominence/gesture shifts leftward when the word-final vowel undergoes coalescence/reduction in hiatus (Franich & Nwosu 2026 'gesture shift'); phrase position also modulates alignment.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level metrical prominence inferred from tonal phonology (downstep resistance in the associative construction) and from gesture-apex alignment in spontaneous interview speech (4 speakers, greater Abuja area); not citation-form stress and not an acoustic stress study. Clark 1990's own wording was not seen (second-hand via these papers).
new_statements.identity_note: Franich et al.'s Igbo data come from four speakers recorded in the greater Abuja area (variety not specified beyond 'Igbo'; examples follow Standard Igbo forms); Clark 1990's analysis is of Standard/Central Igbo (her 1978 data largely Ohuhu/Owerri-area per Green & Igwe tradition). Manfredi 1992 concerns Agbo (Ika area, cf. Glottolog ikaa1238 'Ika'), which Glottolog treats as a separate Igboid language, so it was not used for the statement. Older Ganot 1899 describes Onitsha-area Igbo.

tone_statements.citation: Nwosu, Vincent. 2026. Automatic and non-automatic downstep in Igbo are not realized the same. Proceedings of Speech Prosody 2026, 555-558. ISCA. doi:10.21437/speechprosody.2026-112
tone_statements.quote: Igbo is a terraced-level tone language in which tones occupy an independent representational tier distinct from segmental features [5, 10, 17]. The standard variety contrasts three lexical tones: high (H), low (L), and downstepped high (!H). The high tone is typically realized with elevated pitch, the low tone with depressed pitch, and the downstepped high tone with intermediate pitch that is lower than a preceding high tone but higher than a following low tone [17]. … The mora serves as the tone-bearing unit in Igbo [9].
tone_statements.summary: Terraced-level tone: three lexical tones, high, low and downstepped high; mora the tone-bearing unit; automatic downstep after overt low, non-automatic from a floating low; word stress not discussed.

tone_statements.quote: Ìgbò is a two-tone language with downstep. Because of the relatively small number of tone levels–two levels, while many in Nigeria have three or more levels–Maddieson (2013) classifies it as a simple tone system in the World Atlas of Language Structures. However, previous research on Ìgbò and Yorùbá suggests that the functional load of tone in Ìgbò may be higher than that of Yorùbá. A comparison of two widely available dictionaries [Williamson’s (1972) Ìgbò Dictionary and the University of Ibadan’s Yorùbá Dictionary] revealed that 60% of disyllable entries formed minimal pairs in Ìgbò.

tone_statements.summary: Two tone levels (only 'high' is named) with downstep, a 'terraced' tone language; high functional load of tone; utterance declination treated as phonetic. Stated as background; nothing on word stress.

tone_statements.quote: In a register tone language, tones are essentially level. … An example of a register tone language is Igbo. It has high tone, low tone, down step tone and down drift tone. … There are four different types of tones in Igbo language. They include: High tone, Low tone, Down step, Down drift. But those that are mostly seen in Igbo words include: high tone, low tone, down step. … Igbo language has basically three tones: high tone, low tone and down step. tone_statements.citation: Ezenwafor, Chikelu Ihunanya. 2014. Contour tones in Igbo: 'where they come from'. Theory and Practice in Language Studies 4(4): 661-667. doi:10.4304/tpls.4.4.661-667
tone_statements.quote: Igbo operates a register tone system with two basic level tones (high, low) and a downstep (a reduced high). It also has two contour tones that are not particularly distinctive. Level tones in Igbo function lexically in distinguishing otherwise phonemically identical words. In other words, tone is manipulated contrastively to realize minimal pairs and sets. … Two contour tones are posited for Igbo; the rising (ˇ) and the falling (ˆ) tones. There has been a long tradition of analysing these contours as composite.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 661-662, Section II 'Overview of tone in Igbo'; conclusion on contours as surface composites p. 667, Section VI.
tone_statements.summary: Two level tones, high and low, plus a downstepped (reduced) high; rising and falling contours are non-distinctive surface composites from vowel deletion and floating-tone docking.

tone_statements.quote: An Igbo syllable can have one of three tonal categories, known as “high” (H), “low” (L), “mid” (M). Because the M tone can only occur following an H tone or another M tone, there are five possible tone patterns for two-syllable words … A number of phonologists (e.g. [1]) have interpreted the restricted distribution of the “mid” tone to mean that it is actually a downstepped “high” tone. … downstep is used for the so-called “mid” tone, which is thus considered to be a lowered version of H.

tone_statements.summary: Each syllable is high or low; a 'mid' found only after high is a downstepped high. F0 study: final lows are lowered, downdrift hits H and L alike, and downstep lowers about half as much as downdrift.

In alternating high and low levels (each 00£ which may continue tor one to several syllables), each high level is automatically a little lover th8D. the high level betore the preceding low. tone.quote: Igbo is a "terraced level" tone language. Its tonal system may be described in terms of two tonemes, high and low, plus a phoneme "down-step". In alternating high and low levels (each 00£ which may continue tor one to several syllables), each high level is automatically a little lover th8D. the high level betore the preceding low. The phoneme "down_step" occurs only between two high tones. and has the same lowering effect on the f'ollowing high level that a low tone would have. … It is never possible to go from one non-low level up to a higher non-low level.
